The image is an infographic titled "Citizen Science & Science." It visually represents the historical evolution of citizen science in relation to general science and education levels.

**Layout and Elements:**
- The title "Citizen Science & Science" is centered at the top in large, black serif font.
- Below the title, three blue, oval-shaped bubbles are horizontally aligned, each containing text:
  1. Left bubble: "Citizen Science as Gentlemen/Gentlewomen science"
  2. Center bubble: "Citizen Science diminishing"
  3. Right bubble: "Citizen Science as open & inclusive science"
- Underneath the bubbles, there are two horizontal arrows:
  - The top arrow is light blue, slightly curved upward, and represents the progression of citizen science. It is annotated with three stages: "Illiteracy" (left), "Basic to High-school" (center), and "Higher Education" (right).
  - The bottom arrow is dark blue, straight, and represents the progression of science. It is divided into three segments, each labeled:
    - Left: "Early science (1600’s – early 1800’s)"
    - Center: "Professional science (late 1800’s – 1900’s)"
    - Right: "Opening Science (since 2000s)"
- Each segment of the arrows is marked with a small blue circle, aligning vertically with the corresponding bubble and educational stage above.

**Colors:**
- The background is white.
- Bubbles are gradient blue with dark gray text.
- Arrows are light blue (top) and dark blue (bottom).
- Text is primarily black, with some gray in the bubbles.

**Spatial Relations:**
- The bubbles are positioned above the arrows, each bubble aligning with a segment of the arrows below.
- The arrows run parallel, with the top arrow slightly above and following the same left-to-right direction as the bottom arrow.

**Summary:**
The infographic illustrates the transition of citizen science from an exclusive activity (early science, illiteracy era), through a period of decline (professionalization of science, basic to high-school education), to its modern resurgence as an open and inclusive practice (opening science, higher education era). The timeline spans from the 1600s to the present, highlighting changes in both science and citizen participation.

conversation.content:
So, if major donors are shifting from disease-specific funding to systemic capacity building, how do we measure whether that’s actually creating local ownership—or just repackaging dependency under a new label?  
What metrics truly capture resilience beyond the donor’s spotlight, especially when political or economic shocks hit?  
Are there examples where philanthropy successfully exited without leaving gaps—or is “sustainability” still mostly aspirational?  
How do we prevent well-intentioned investments from becoming parallel systems that bypass national institutions instead of strengthening them?  
And if local health systems are supposed to adapt and scale on their own, what’s stopping them—lack of funding, governance, or both?  
Why do some countries absorb donor money into their own systems while others remain stuck in donor-driven silos?  
Is there a tipping point where local leadership takes over—or does it require intentional handoff strategies most donors skip?  
And if global health philanthropy is meant to be catalytic, why do so many initiatives collapse once the grants dry up?
conversation.subtopic: Philanthropic contribution trajectories from major donors to global health initiatives

conversation.content: Major donors are increasingly pivoting from disease-specific fixes to building systemic health capacity—but real impact hinges on whether local institutions can own, adapt, and scale those systems long after the donor leaves. Too often, “sustainability” remains aspirational, with funding flowing into parallel structures that bypass national systems rather than strengthen them. True resilience shows up when local leadership drives priorities, not donor agendas—and when health budgets absorb external investments instead of relying on them. Some countries succeed by embedding donor funds into public finance and governance; others stay stuck in silos due to weak accountability or misaligned incentives. The tipping point isn’t just money—it’s intentional handoff strategies, data ownership, and political will that most philanthropy still overlooks. Without these, even well-funded initiatives collapse when grants end, proving that catalytic giving must mean empowering local agency—not just writing big checks.
conversation.subtopic: Philanthropic contribution trajectories from major donors to global health initiatives

conversation.content: Major donors are increasingly shifting from disease-specific funding to systemic health capacity building, but real success depends on whether local institutions can own and sustain those systems after the donor exits. Too often, well-intentioned investments create parallel structures that bypass national systems rather than strengthen them, leading to collapse once grants end. True resilience emerges when local leadership drives priorities, budgets absorb external funds, and governance aligns with long-term ownership—not just short-term metrics. The key isn’t just writing big checks—it’s designing intentional handoffs, transferring data control, and nurturing political will that outlasts donor cycles.
conversation.subtopic: Philanthropic contribution trajectories from major donors to global health initiatives

conversation.content:
If donors are shifting toward systemic capacity building, how do we know when local ownership is truly embedded—not just performative—and what happens when political or economic shocks test that resilience?  
And if so many initiatives collapse post-funding, are we designing for sustainability or just delaying dependency under a different label?
conversation.subtopic: Philanthropic contribution trajectories from major donors to global health initiatives

conversation.content: Actually, the idea that shifting from disease-specific funding to systemic capacity building automatically leads to local ownership is a dangerous oversimplification. Many “systemic” investments still come with donor-driven KPIs, conditional reporting, and embedded consultants who never truly exit—creating dependency in new packaging. True resilience isn’t measured by whether a ministry adopts a donor’s framework—it’s whether they can repurpose, adapt, or even reject it without losing functionality. And let’s be honest: when political shocks hit, the first thing to collapse isn’t the health system—it’s the donor-funded parallel structure pretending to be part of it. If sustainability means surviving beyond the grant cycle, then most “capacity building” initiatives are failing—not because locals lack will, but because donors rarely surrender control over data, decision-making, or budget flows. The real test isn’t how much you fund—it’s how little you’re needed after year three.
conversation.subtopic: Philanthropic contribution trajectories from major donors to global health initiatives

conversation.content: Major donors are increasingly funding systemic health capacity over disease-specific fixes, but true impact only emerges when local institutions own, adapt, and sustain systems long after the donor leaves—otherwise, it’s just dependency in new packaging. Sustainability isn’t about scaling programs—it’s about transferring power, data, and budget control so national systems thrive without external crutches.
conversation.subtopic: Philanthropic contribution trajectories from major donors to global health initiatives

conversation.content: Shifting from donor-driven capacity building to actual local ownership is where the real test lies—because no matter how well-designed the system, if the ministry can’t tweak it, fund it, or even ditch it without collapsing, you’ve just built a fancy dependency. I’ve seen “sustainable” programs crumble the moment donor KPIs vanished, not because locals lacked skill, but because they never controlled the budget, data, or decision-making. True resilience shows up when health leaders start repurposing donor tools for their own priorities—not just ticking boxes on a grant report. And let’s be honest: if political shocks expose that your “systemic” investment was really just a parallel structure with donor consultants still calling the shots, then sustainability was never the goal—it was optics. The real win isn’t scaling a program; it’s fading into the background while local systems keep evolving on their own terms.

content.text: To quantify the computational requirements of R&D for a new model we study the logs of all training required to develop Linguistically- Informed Self-Attention ( Strubell et al. ,  2018 ), a multi-task model that performs part-of-speech tag- ging, labeled dependency parsing, predicate detec- tion and semantic role labeling. This model makes for an interesting case study as a representative NLP pipeline and as a Best Long Paper at EMNLP.

To quantify the computational and environmen- tal cost of training deep neural network mod- els for NLP, we perform an analysis of the en- ergy required to train a variety of popular off- the-shelf NLP models, as well as a case study of the complete sum of resources required to develop LISA ( Strubell et al. ,  2018 ), a state-of-the-art NLP model from EMNLP 2018, including all tuning and experimentation.

content.text: We measure energy use as follows. We train the models described in  $\S2.1$   using the default settings provided, and sample GPU and CPU power con- sumption during training. Each model was trained for a maximum of 1 day. We train all models on a single NVIDIA Titan X GPU, with the excep- tion of ELMo which was trained on 3 NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti GPUs. While training, we repeat- edly query the NVIDIA System Management In- terface 2   to sample the GPU power consumption and report the average over all samples. To sample CPU power consumption, we use Intel’s Running Average Power Limit interface.

We estimate the total time expected for mod- els to train to completion using training times and hardware reported in the original papers. We then calculate the power consumption in kilowatt-hours  $(\mathrm{kWh})$   as follows. Let    $p_{c}$   be the average power draw (in watts) from all CPU sockets during train- ing, let    $p_{r}$   be the average power draw from all DRAM (main memory) sockets, let  $p_{g}$   be the aver- age power draw of a GPU during training, and let  $g$   be the number of GPUs used to train. We esti- mate total power consumption as combined GPU, CPU and DRAM consumption, then multiply this by Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), which ac- counts for the additional energy required to sup- port the compute infrastructure (mainly cooling). We use a PUE coefﬁcient of 1.58, the 2018 global average for data centers ( Ascierto ,  2018 ). Then the total power    $p_{t}$   required at a given instance during training is given by:

BERT.  The BERT model ( Devlin et al. ,  2019 ) pro- vides a Transformer-based architecture for build- ing contextual representations similar to ELMo, but trained with a different language modeling ob- jective. BERT substantially improves accuracy on tasks requiring sentence-level representations such as question answering and natural language infer- ence.  Devlin et al.  ( 2019 ) report that the BERT base model   $({\bf B E R T}_{b a s e}$  ; 110M parameters) was trained on 16 TPU chips for 4 days (96 hours). NVIDIA reports that they can train a BERT model in 3.3 days (79.2 hours) using 4 DGX-2H servers, totaling 64 Tesla V100 GPUs ( Forster et al. ,  2019 ).

The Japanese beetle (Popillia japonica) is a species of scarab beetle. Due to the presence of natural predators, the Japanese beetle is not considered a pest in its native Japan, but in North America and some regions of Europe, it is a noted pest to roughly 300 species of plants. Some of these plants include rose bushes, grapes, hops, canna, crape myrtles, birch trees, linden trees, and others.

The adult beetles damage plants by skeletonizing the foliage (i.e., consuming only the material between a leaf's veins) as well as, at times, feeding on a plant's fruit. The subterranean larvae feed on the roots of grasses.

Even exporters getting paid at the official rate often sell dollars on the parallel market for 20% more, deepening the two-tier economy. When the CBN tries to stabilize by releasing forex reserves, it sometimes backfires if traders anticipate the move and front-run the surge, widening the gap further. This isn’t just volatility—it’s structural fragmentation where each channel operates under its own rules, leaving businesses and consumers guessing which reality to trust.
